title: Vegetables
description: Name the vegetables, and learn the two that break the ending rule.
grammar: gender and articles, and the plural of nouns
grammarNote: Vegetables are mostly feminine, and the two most common ones are the exceptions.

explanation.summary: Vegetable names are the same kind of noun as fruit names, with one trap: the two you meet first, la patata and el tomate, are the ones that do not follow the ending rule.

sections.heading: The nouns
sections.body: La patata, la cebolla, la zanahoria, la lechuga and la espinaca are feminine. El tomate, el pimiento, el guisante, el brócoli and el calabacín are masculine. El tomate is the one to remember: it ends in -o, so it is masculine, but la patata ends in -a and is still feminine. The ending is only a guide.

sections.heading: Plurals with a twist
sections.body: The plural adds -s or -es as usual: las patatas, los tomates, las zanahorias. Two words lose their ending: el brócoli becomes los brócolis and el calabacín becomes los calabacines. In the kitchen you say verduras for all of them at once.

items.note: Feminine: la patata. The plural is las patatas.
Masculine: el calabacín. The accent marks the stress.
Masculine: el brócoli. The plural is los brócolis.

drills.note: Patata is feminine, so las patatas.

drills.meaning: I need two lettuces from the greengrocer
drills.note: Léchuga is feminine, so las lechugas.
